copy.pageTitle: 100 Days of Python Code — Curriculum & Learning Path
copy.title: 100 days of python code
copy.deck: One hundred consecutive days, each one a single sitting: something to learn, something to build. Starts at installing Python, ends with a deployed full-stack app and a package on PyPI. No day depends on anything you haven't already written yourself.

closing.p: Finish the build before you close the editor, then commit it. The repo becomes the proof — a hundred small, dated, working programs.
Skipping the build is not. The order matters far more than the calendar; pick the streak back up on the day you left it.
Reading Python is not writing Python. Every concept listed on a day should appear in something you typed yourself that day.
When a build works, change one thing until it fails, and read the traceback. Ten extra minutes here is worth an hour of tutorials.

copy.footer: 100 Days of Python Code — curriculum & learning path

phases.name: Foundations
phases.outcome: Get Python running and get comfortable with the four things every later day is made of: values, names, expressions and output. No libraries, no frameworks — just you and the interpreter.

phases.name: Control flow
phases.outcome: Teach your programs to decide and repeat. By the end of this phase you can express any procedure a human could follow by hand.

phases.name: Data structures
phases.outcome: Stop juggling loose variables. Learn the four containers Python programs are actually built out of, and which one to reach for when.
phases.milestone: An expense tracker with monthly reports

phases.name: Functions & modular code
phases.outcome: Turn scripts into reusable pieces. Arguments, scope, decorators and generators — the tools that let a program grow past one file without collapsing.

phases.name: Object-oriented Python
phases.outcome: Model the problem instead of the procedure. Classes, dunder methods and dataclasses — plus when not to use inheritance, which matters more than the syntax.

phases.name: Robust code
phases.outcome: The phase that separates scripts from software: errors you handle, files you read, tests that prove it works, and types that catch mistakes before you run it.
phases.milestone: A fully tested, typed CLI tool

phases.name: The outside world
phases.outcome: Python's real advantage is its standard library and its ecosystem. Dates, regex, HTTP, real CLIs, logging, environments and Git — the working day-to-day kit.

phases.name: Data & analysis
phases.outcome: Handle data at a scale loops can't. NumPy for arrays, pandas for tables, matplotlib for the picture, SQL for the source — and a written conclusion at the end.

phases.name: Web & APIs
phases.outcome: Put your work behind a URL. Flask for pages, FastAPI for services, SQLAlchemy for storage, auth for users — and a real deployment at the end of it.

phases.name: Scale & craft
phases.outcome: The professional layer: concurrency, profiling, packaging, CI and code review. Ends with a project that is entirely yours, shipped the way real projects ship.

days.b: A program that prints your name inside an ASCII frame it draws to fit.
A temperature converter that handles Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin in both directions.
An initials extractor that turns any full name into a set of initials.
A receipt printer that aligns item names, quantities and prices into clean columns.
A bill splitter that handles tips, uneven shares and rounds to real currency.

k: why input is always a string
days.b: An interactive BMI calculator that refuses nonsense input instead of crashing.
A password strength checker that reports which rules a password fails.
Take a deliberately ugly 60-line script and refactor it until ruff is silent.
Five broken scripts, five bugs. Fix all of them and write down what each error meant.
A ten-question quiz that asks, scores, gives feedback per answer and prints a final grade.
A grade calculator that turns any percentage into a letter, with boundary cases handled.
A number guessing game that gives higher/lower hints and counts attempts.
A multiplication table generator that lines up perfectly for any size you ask for.
A prime number finder that stops checking the moment it knows the answer.
An ASCII art generator: pyramids, diamonds and a chessboard, all from nested loops.
A dice simulator that rolls ten thousand times and plots the distribution as text bars.
A command parser that turns typed instructions like 'go north' into actions.
Compute mean, median, mode, min and max over a list — without importing anything.
A Pomodoro timer that counts down in place and rings when the interval ends.
A multi-room adventure with an inventory, locked doors and at least two endings.
A to-do list you can add to, complete, reorder and delete from, all in memory.
Rewrite ten explicit loops as comprehensions, then rewrite two of them back and say why.
A geometry helper: distance, midpoint and area, all passing points around as tuples.
A contact book with lookup by name, partial search and safe handling of missing entries.
A word frequency analyser that reports the top twenty words in any text file.
A duplicate finder that also reports what two tag lists share and where they differ.
A leaderboard sorted by score descending, then by time ascending, then alphabetically.
Read a deeply nested config structure and answer five questions about it without crashing.
Benchmark membership tests across a list, a set and a dict at three sizes; explain the curve.
Track expenses by category and month, then print a report with totals and the biggest spend.
A personal library of ten small utilities you will actually reuse later in the course.
A report generator whose defaults make the common call one argument long.
A wrapper that logs every call — its name, its arguments and what it returned.
A counter factory and a memo cache, both built from closures instead of classes.
The same data pipeline written three ways — loop, comprehension, functional — then judged.
A directory tree walker that prints an indented listing of any folder you point it at.
Write @timer, @retry and @cache, then apply them to your Day 31 utilities.
Stream a 500 MB log file and count error lines without ever loading it into memory.
Split your utilities into a proper package with submodules and a clean public surface.
Package your best helpers into one importable library with documentation and examples.
A BankAccount class that deposits, withdraws, refuses overdrafts and keeps a history.
An Employee class that issues sequential IDs and can be built from a CSV row.
A Vector class that prints usefully, compares correctly and works inside a set.
A Money type that adds, compares and sorts — and refuses to mix currencies silently.
A shape hierarchy where every subclass computes its own area behind one shared interface.
Take a four-level inheritance chain and rebuild it from small collaborating objects.
A Temperature class where setting an impossible value raises instead of quietly storing it.
Rewrite three of your earlier classes as dataclasses and count the lines you deleted.
A plugin interface with two working implementations that the caller can't tell apart.
Model products, stock and orders as objects, with a menu-driven interface over the top.
A safe input reader that survives bad types, empty input and Ctrl-C without a traceback.

k: error messages people can act on
days.b: A validation layer for your inventory system with domain-specific error types.
A log splitter that breaks one large file into daily files without loading it all at once.
Clean a CSV with missing fields and inconsistent casing, then write a summary CSV back out.
A settings store that loads defaults, merges user overrides and saves changes to disk.
A bulk renamer with a dry-run mode that shows every change before it touches anything.
Write a real test suite for the toolkit you built on Day 40 and find at least one bug.
Table-driven tests for your validators, plus a mocked clock so time-based code is testable.
Annotate your whole package and drive mypy to zero errors without using Any as an escape.
A file-processing tool with a test suite above 90% coverage, full type hints and a README.
An age and countdown calculator that gets leap years and time zones right.
Pull every email address, date and IP out of a messy raw text dump into a clean report.
Give your Day 60 tool a real CLI with subcommands, --help and correct exit statuses.
Replace every print in one of your projects with structured logging to console and file.
A weather CLI that takes a city and prints a formatted forecast from a public API.
Fetch a fully paginated dataset, cache it locally and never re-request what you already have.
Scrape a book catalogue into a CSV — title, price, rating — across multiple pages.
Give every project you have built so far a reproducible environment someone else can install.
Put the whole hundred-day repo under version control with a commit for each day so far.
Pull live data from two APIs, cache it, and render a formatted dashboard in the terminal.
Load an image as an array and produce greyscale, inverted and cropped versions of it.
A full grade analytics report — per student, per subject, per cohort — with no Python loops.
Load a real public dataset and produce a one-page profile of what is actually in it.
Take a deliberately messy sales export and get it to the point where every column is trustworthy.
Revenue by region by quarter, with growth rates, from a single grouped expression.
Combine three separate exports into one analysis-ready table and prove no rows were lost.
A four-panel figure where every panel supports the same single conclusion.
Load your dataset into SQLite and answer the same five questions in SQL and in pandas.
Redo one earlier analysis as a notebook that reads as an argument, not a pile of cells.
Pick a dataset, ask one real question, and answer it with charts and a written conclusion.
Map an API you already use into a table of endpoints, methods, inputs and responses.
A personal portfolio site with a shared layout and a page for each project you have built.
A guestbook that accepts entries, rejects bad ones with useful messages and remembers you.
Move the guestbook off memory and onto a real database, with a migration to prove it.
A complete CRUD API for your Day 50 inventory model, with generated interactive docs.
Add signup, login and per-user data to your API — with passwords you could safely leak.
A test suite that covers every endpoint including the failure paths, not just the happy ones.
A small JavaScript front end that reads and writes through your API in the browser.
Containerise the API and ship it to a public URL that someone else can hit.
One deployed application with accounts, persistent data and a UI — live, on the internet.
Run one I/O workload and one CPU workload three ways each and chart which approach wins.
A parallel downloader that fetches fifty files at once and reports live progress.
Process a folder of images across every core and measure the real speed-up you got.
Fetch a hundred URLs concurrently and compare the wall-clock time against the threaded version.
Profile your slowest script, make it ten times faster, and show the before-and-after numbers.

k: when a function beats a class
days.b: Refactor the inventory system with one pattern that removes real duplication, not just structure.
Publish your toolkit so that pip install works from a clean machine.
A pipeline that runs your tests, linter and type checker on every push and blocks on failure.
Open one real pull request against an open-source Python project — docs count.

days.t: Capstone — ship something of your own
days.b: Your idea, built and shipped: tested, documented, deployed, and written up so others can use it.
